analysis.one_liner: Lets health insurers once again cap how much they will pay for a person's care over a lifetime.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with no cosponsors and no vote, so the ACA's ban on lifetime coverage caps stayed in place.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the part of the 2010 health care law (the Affordable Care Act) that stops insurance plans from putting a lifetime dollar limit on the care a person can receive. Before the ACA, insurers could cut off payment for a patient's care after costs passed a cap, no matter how sick they were. The bill died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurers, who would regain the ability to cap the total benefits they pay for any one customer over a lifetime, limiting their costs for the most expensive patients.

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the Affordable Care Act's ban on lifetime dollar limits on benefits, allowing insurers to cap what they will pay for any one person's care over their lifetime.
That would let health plans cap their exposure on the most expensive patients, which the bill's sponsor framed as repealing part of the 2010 health reform law.

analysis.who_pays: Seriously ill people, who would once again risk having their insurance stop paying after a lifetime cap is reached, leaving them uninsured for further care.

drawbacks.text: It would again allow insurers to place lifetime dollar caps on benefits, so a person with a serious illness could exhaust their coverage and be left with no insurance exactly when care is most expensive.
The repeal takes effect immediately upon enactment, so coverage caps could return without any transition period for people mid-treatment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The drawbacks are serious and the benefits are essentially none for the public: the bill takes away a newly won protection for the sickest patients and hands insurers a tool for capping their costs, with nothing in exchange. It was never voted on, so no one bore the cost in practice.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, and Congress ended a few weeks later with no vote ever taken.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 29, 2010 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the same day.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never voted on it and the full House never considered it.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained ground from the outcome itself, but health insurers remain the beneficiary of the bill's failure to attract support, since the ACA's ban on lifetime caps stayed in force.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill simply expired

for.name: Rep. Gary Ackerman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the ACA's ban on lifetime benefit limits.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral, and it never received a markup or a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single sponsor and no cosponsors and never reached a vote, so no party bloc ever took a position on it.

industries.note: Repealing the ban on lifetime limits would let insurers cap the dollar value of benefits per customer, limiting their cost for policyholders with expensive illnesses. The cost falls on seriously ill people, whose coverage could run out.
